name: Teo Rotating Traversable Wormhole
description: Edward Teo's rotating traversable wormhole of 1998, the stationary, axially symmetric generalisation of the Morris-Thorne wormhole, in the example he worked out. Exotic matter still holds its throat open, some travellers fall through without meeting any, and a fast enough spin wraps the equator of the throat in an ergoregion.
convention: The throat radius $b_0$ is a length, and the spin $a = GJ/(c^3b_0^2)$ is the angular momentum $J$ in units of the throat, a pure number. We keep factors of $c$ explicit. The Ricci tensor is the standard contraction, $R_{\mu\nu} = R^\alpha{}_{\mu\alpha\nu}$.
history: What would a wormhole look like if somebody built one? Edward Teo guessed in 1998 that the work of an arbitrarily advanced civilization "would in all likelihood be aspherical or rotating" [teo1998]. Michael Morris and Kip Thorne's wormhole of ten years earlier was static and spherically symmetric, and every traveller through it has to cross the exotic matter holding its throat open [morris1988, teo1998]. Matt Visser showed in 1989, with flat space cut and joined along thin shells, that a wormhole without spherical symmetry can keep its exotic matter out of a traveller's way [visser1989prd]. Teo wanted the same for a wormhole that turns, so that travellers could "avoid passing through and interacting with the exotic matter needed to maintain the wormhole" [teo1998].¶He kept the method of Morris and Thorne: write the geometry down first, then ask the Einstein equations what matter it needs [teo1998, morris1988]. A stationary, axisymmetric metric has four free functions of $r$ and $\theta$, and Teo put it in James Hartle's 1967 form for rotating stars, $ds^2 = -N^2c^2dt^2 + (1 - b/r)^{-1}dr^2 + r^2K^2\left(d\theta^2 + \sin^2\theta\left(d\phi - \omega\,dt\right)^2\right)$ [teo1998, hartle1967]. The redshift function $N$ has to stay finite and nonzero, since a zero of $N$ is a horizon [teo1998]. The shape function $b$ is Morris and Thorne's, with the throat at $r = b$, while $K$ sets the size of the circles about the axis and $\omega$ is the angular velocity of a particle falling freely from infinity [teo1998]. With $\omega = 0$, $K = 1$, and nothing depending on $\theta$, the metric is the Morris-Thorne wormhole again [teo1998].¶Teo proved that the null energy condition fails somewhere on the throat of every such wormhole, and concluded that "one can never avoid the use of exotic matter altogether" [teo1998]. The exotic matter can be moved around the throat, though, and he built an example to show it: $N = K = 1 + (4a\cos\theta)^2/r$, $b = 1$, and $\omega = 2a/r^3$ in units of the throat radius, with $a$ the angular momentum [teo1998]. Its throat is narrowest at the equator and widens toward the poles, a shape he called "dumbbell-like" [teo1998]. At $a = 1/4$ a light ray falling in along the equatorial plane with no angular momentum has $R_{ab}k^ak^b = E^2/r^3$, positive all the way through [teo1998]. A massive particle on the same path meets no negative energy density either, once its energy per unit rest mass passes about $1.75$ [teo1998].¶Spun faster, the example grows an ergoregion: for $|a| > 1/2$ the component $g_{tt}$ turns positive in a region outside the throat, where no particle can stay at rest with respect to infinity [teo1998]. The region stops short of the poles and forms what Teo called a "tube" around the equator, since an ergoregion reaching the poles would have to meet a horizon there, and a traversable wormhole has none [teo1998]. That makes the traditional name of ergosphere, he remarked, "hardly appropriate here" [teo1998]. Roger Penrose had shown in 1969 how a particle breaking up inside the ergoregion of a rotating black hole can leave with more energy than went in, and Teo pointed out that the same process draws rotational energy from his wormhole [penrose1969, teo1998]. Naoki Tsukamoto and Cosimo Bambi showed in 2015 that the example with a small throat accelerates particles: two of them meeting head on at the throat collide at a high energy in their centre of mass frame, with no fine tuning of their angular momenta [tsukamoto2015]. They called it "the first example of particle collision with high center-of-mass energy in a spacetime with no event horizon, no naked singularity, and not being extremal in a clear sense" [tsukamoto2015].¶What kind of matter could be the source of Teo's wormhole? Santiago Perez Bergliaffa and K. E. Hibberd put the question in 2000 and found that the example cannot be the field of a perfect fluid, or of a fluid with anisotropic stresses [perezbergliaffa2000]. Its source must carry something more, they concluded, "for example heat flux" [perezbergliaffa2000]. With the angular velocity allowed to change in time, Peter Kuhfittig found in 2003 a violation of the weak energy condition "considerably less severe than in the static spherically symmetric case" [kuhfittig2003]. The Ellis wormhole, with its phantom scalar field as the source, can be set rotating too: Burkhard Kleihaus and Jutta Kunz solved the Einstein equations for it numerically in 2014, and noted that the Teo wormhole "is not a solution of the Einstein-matter equations" [kleihaus2014]. Their wormholes spin up only so far: at the greatest rotation a degenerate horizon forms at the throat and the family ends in an extremal Kerr black hole [kleihaus2014].¶Astrophysicists have since used Teo's metric as their model of a spinning wormhole [harko2009, nedkova2013, shaikh2018]. A thin accretion disk around such a wormhole turns about half of the accreted mass into radiation, more than the 42 percent of an extreme Kerr black hole, as Tiberiu Harko, Zoltán Kovács, and Francisco Lobo found in 2009 [harko2009]. The shadow of a rotating wormhole of Teo's form is nearly Kerr's at small angular momentum and considerably different at large, by the computation of Petya Nedkova, Vassil Tinchev, and Stoytcho Yazadjiev in 2013 [nedkova2013]. Those shadows were incomplete, Rajibul Shaikh showed in 2018, since light can also circle at the throat itself, and he drew the complete ones [shaikh2018].

related.text: Teo's wormhole with the spin taken out. With $\omega = 0$, $K = 1$, and nothing depending on $\theta$ his canonical metric is the Morris-Thorne one, and his example at $a = 0$ is its member $\Phi = 0$, $b = b_0$ [teo1998].

The static wormhole held open by a phantom scalar field. Burkhard Kleihaus and Jutta Kunz set its throat rotating in 2014 and solved the field equations numerically, which gave rotating wormholes whose matter is known [kleihaus2014].

A rotating geometry with an ergoregion, as Teo's is for $|a| > 1/2$. Kerr's ergoregion encloses a horizon, Teo's is a tube round the equator of a throat, and the Penrose process draws energy from either [teo1998, penrose1969].

Matt Visser's cut and paste wormhole. In the same year he showed, with flat space cut along a polyhedron, that a traveller can cross a wormhole and miss its exotic matter, which is what Teo wanted from rotation [visser1989prd, teo1998].

coordinates.convention: We use Teo's coordinates $(t, r, \theta, \phi)$, with $t$ carrying dimensions of time, and his redshift function $N$ and his $K$ are both $1 + 16a^2b_0\cos^2\theta/r$. We take components in the chart $x^0 = ct$, and a dot in the geodesic equations is a derivative with respect to an affine parameter, so $\dot{t}$ means $d(ct)/d\lambda$.
